name: Hearthstone Firearms Model 9 'Payday'
description:
The Hearthstone Model 9 is a bottom-of-the-barrel semi-automatic pistol chambered in 9x19mm, manufactured from injection-molded polymer and stamped steel components. The barrel is unrifled on early production runs — a cost-cutting measure that Hearthstone has never officially acknowledged. The trigger pull is heavy and gritty, the sights are rudimentary plastic posts, and the magazine release has a documented tendency to drop magazines under recoil.

The Payday is the firearm of last resort for people who cannot afford anything better. It is sold in blister packs at convenience stores in Shelf districts, often alongside prepaid comm cards and synthetic protein bars. Shelf security forces confiscate thousands annually, but the economics of the weapon make replacement trivial — a new Model 9 costs less than a decent meal in the Mids.

Despite its reputation as disposable junk, the Payday has an outsized cultural presence. It appears in countless Shelf folk songs and street poetry as a symbol of desperation and defiance. The phrase 'pulling a Payday' has entered common slang meaning to attempt something with inadequate tools and pure nerve.
specifications:
caliber: 9x19mm
effective_range: 15 meters
rate_of_fire: Semi-automatic
magazine_capacity: 8 rounds
weight: 0.45 kg
tactical_use: The Model 9 is not a tactical weapon in any meaningful sense. It is a point-blank defensive tool with poor accuracy beyond conversational distance. Users who carry it do so because they have no other option. In a confrontation, the best strategy is to close distance and fire rapidly, hoping volume compensates for the weapon's inherent inaccuracy.
cultural_context: In Shelf culture, the Payday is simultaneously mocked and respected — mocked for its quality, respected for what carrying one implies about the owner's circumstances and willingness to fight regardless. Corponation marketing campaigns occasionally appropriate Shelf gun culture imagery, which is universally regarded as tasteless.
known_users: First-time gun owners with no budget
story_hooks: A character finds a Payday with one round left in a dead courier's hand — and the serial number has been scratched off with something that wasn't a tool.
A Shelf community organizer is buying Paydays in bulk, but not for the reason anyone assumes.

physical_description.visual_profile: A blocky, utilitarian semi-automatic pistol with aggressive angularity and no aesthetic pretense. The profile reads cheap and mass-produced—all sharp edges and functional geometry with no flourishes. The frame dominates visually, appearing slightly too large for the proportions, while the slide seems thin and stamped rather than milled. At first glance it reads as a tool, not a weapon—the kind of thing you'd expect to find in a clearance bin.
physical_description.dimensions: Overall length: 19.5 cm | Slide width: 3.2 cm | Grip height: 10.8 cm | Barrel length: 9.7 cm (unrifled)
physical_description.weight_description: Light and hollow-feeling, with an unpleasant plasticky responsiveness to movement. Carries with a tinny quality—more rattle than presence. Feels cheaper in hand than its already-minimal price suggests, lacking the reassuring heft of even mid-tier firearms.
physical_description.primary_material: Injection-molded polymer frame (cheap virgin plastic, not recycled) with stamped steel slide and barrel. Springs and internals are similarly cost-reduced steel stampings.
physical_description.finish: Industrial matte gray polymer with dull black stamped steel slide. The finish is functionally absent—no coating, no polish. Bare injection mold marks visible on the frame. Early scuffing from packaging and handling appears even on 'new' units.
physical_description.color_scheme: Institutional gray polymer with flat black steel components. No accent colors or branding polish—purely utilitarian corporate monochrome.
physical_description.grip_texture: Rough injection-molded polymer with minimal texturing—almost slick when gloved, prone to sweat-slip. The grip is slightly too wide for comfort and has sharp edges where the polymer seams don't blend cleanly. No grip panels or aftermarket upgrades appear on stock units.
distinctive_features: Rudimentary plastic post sights—white paint worn and chipped
Magazine release with visible manufacturing flash
Unrifled barrel (early runs) creating visible bore striations
Stamped steel slide with visible tool marks from production
No safety markings or indicator dots
Heavy, gritty trigger visible through frame gaps
Magazine well designed for friction fit rather than positive retention
Serial number stamped in tiny digits on the slide, difficult to read
Tiny Hearthstone logo heat-stamped into polymer frame, already fading
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: Tiny 'HEARTHSTONE FIREARMS' text molded into grip panel (often upside-down from mold orientation). Serial number stamped into slide in 0.8mm font. No other markings. No safety or caliber warnings printed anywhere.
physical_description.condition_typical: Shelf-worn even when 'new'—packaging wear, minor scuffs, loose muzzle crown from handling. Paint already beginning to fade on sights. Magazine springs show slight compression set. The 'well-maintained' version of this weapon still looks neglected; the 'battle-worn' version is indistinguishable.
